claim: The ILO and the Oxford Internet Institute's Online Labour Observatory estimate that of 163 million registered platform accounts only 8.6 percent are active and just 2 percent have completed at least ten projects or earned at least US$1,000.
stance_target: The position that only a low-single-digit percentage of people who register to earn on a platform ever reach a meaningful cumulative income threshold
scope_conditions: Global; web-based online gig platforms (freelancing and microtask), explicitly NOT content-creation platforms; attributed to the Online Labour Observatory with no sample size or reference year stated in the citing text; published as ILO Working Paper 164 for Asia and the Pacific
quoted_support: The Online Labour Observatory of the Oxford Internet Institute and the International Labour Organization (ILO) estimate there are 163 million registered user accounts, with 8.6 per cent of them "active" and 2 per cent having completed at least ten projects or earned at least US$1,000.
time_period: not stated in source; underlying estimate traces to Kassi, Lehdonvirta and Stephany 2021

claim: No systematic measurement of platform-worker numbers exists across Asia and the Pacific, and most countries in the region do not collect the data at all.
stance_target: The position that Southeast Asian quantitative evidence on platform and creator work is structurally absent rather than merely unsearched, so Western figures cannot be validated against local baselines
scope_conditions: Asia and the Pacific region; as of the paper's writing (ILO Working Paper 164); refers to enterprise surveys and labour force surveys
quoted_support: There is no systematic data collection across the region on the number of workers carrying out work via digital labour platforms. To date, only a limited number of enterprise surveys or labour force surveys have systematically captured the number of digital platform workers.

claim: Platform workers constitute 4 per cent of the employed population in the Philippines, against 2.4 per cent of the non-farm workforce in India and over 10 per cent of the workforce in China having ever participated.
stance_target: The size of the platform-work population in Asian economies relative to the total labour force
scope_conditions: Philippines, China, India; China figures for 2015 and 2020; India figure 6.8 million gig workers; measures all digital labour platform work including ride-hailing and delivery, not content creation
quoted_support: In the Philippines, data suggests that platform workers constitute 4 per cent of the employed population.
numbers: 6.5 per cent to over 10 per cent China workforce

claim: ASEAN estimates 63 million registered workers in online freelancing services and roughly 40 million in on-demand digital services, a registration-based count with no active-worker adjustment.
stance_target: The reliability of headline Southeast Asian platform-worker counts
scope_conditions: ASEAN member states; ASEAN Secretariat 2023; registered accounts, not active workers, so the 8.6 percent active adjustment in the same paragraph would imply a far smaller working population
quoted_support: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) estimates suggest that there are 63 million registered workers engaged in online freelancing services and roughly 40 million in on-demand digital services.

claim: Roughly 66 per cent of Asia-Pacific workers (1.3 billion people) depend on the informal economy, rising to 71 per cent in emerging economies versus 22 per cent in advanced economies, so the counterfactual against which platform or creator income should be judged is fundamentally different in Southeast Asia than in the West.
stance_target: The position that US and Western creator-income and living-wage benchmarks do not transfer to Southeast Asia
scope_conditions: Asia and the Pacific; ILO informality statistics; contrasted with advanced economies
quoted_support: Almost 66 per cent, or 1.3 billion workers in Asia and the Pacific rely on the informal economy
